The [Provo measurements](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) define each response as a mean log first fixation duration aggregated across readers and modeled cloze surprisal as the negative base 2 logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. The regression specifies a straight conditional mean for those summaries. We now need an estimation rule. **Ordinary least squares (OLS)** chooses the coefficients whose fitted values minimize the residual sum of squares. This is the squared error rule introduced for the observed sample; the [maximum likelihood connection](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) comes after the minimizer is derived.

Here a [**residual**](residuals.qmd) provisionally means $y_i-\widehat y_i$, the observed response minus its fitted value. The Gaussian likelihood factors over rows only under the stated [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption, and its [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) controls the scale of squared error.

We first derive the squared error objective and its minimizer, then compute the Provo estimate and reconnect the resulting rule to its sampling assumptions.

The basic idea is to try a line, measure every vertical discrepancy, and then adjust the line until the sum of the squared discrepancies cannot be made smaller. Squaring serves two purposes in this calculation: it prevents a positive discrepancy $e$ and a negative discrepancy $-e$ from canceling, and it gives a larger discrepancy more weight. Their combined squared contribution is $e^2+(-e)^2=2e^2$.

## From discrepancies to an objective

For candidate coefficients $b_0$ and $b_1$, define

$$
\widetilde y_i(b_0,b_1)=b_0+b_1x_i
$$

and

$$
e_i(b_0,b_1)=y_i-\widetilde y_i(b_0,b_1).
$$

The OLS objective is

$$
Q(b_0,b_1)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i\right)^2.
$$

We use $b_0$ and $b_1$ while considering arbitrary candidate lines, then place hats on $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ for the candidates that minimize $Q$. This notation lets us distinguish the values being tried from the estimates selected by the rule.

We now use a [derivative](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change), which measures how a quantity changes under a very small change in its input. Here a partial derivative changes one coefficient while holding the other fixed. A positive derivative says that increasing that coefficient raises squared error locally; a negative derivative says that increasing it lowers squared error locally. Differentiate one coefficient at a time:

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_0}
=-2\sum_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i),
$$

$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_1}
=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i).
$$

At the minimizer both derivatives are zero. The equations obtained by setting
these derivatives to zero are called the **normal equations**. The first normal
equation gives

$$
\sum_i y_i=n\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1\sum_i x_i,
$$

so

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\overline y-\widehat\beta_1\overline x.
$$

Substitute this expression into the second normal equation:

$$
0
=
\sum_i x_i
\left[
(y_i-\overline y)
-\widehat\beta_1(x_i-\overline x)
\right].
$$

Because the centered terms sum to zero, this is equivalent to

$$
\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)
=
\widehat\beta_1
\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2.
$$

Thus

$$
\widehat\beta_1
=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2}
$$

This formula requires at least two distinct observed predictor values, so that
$\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2>0$. Under that condition the squared error objective
curves upward in every coefficient direction. The solution at which both
derivatives equal zero is therefore the unique minimum rather than a maximum or
a flat region.

To verify that claim, differentiate both normal equations once more. The matrix
of second derivatives, called the [**Hessian**](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature), is

$$
\nabla^2Q
=
2
\begin{bmatrix}
n & \sum_i x_i\\
\sum_i x_i & \sum_i x_i^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For any proposed coefficient direction
$\mathbf a=(a_0,a_1)^\mathsf T$, its curvature in that direction is

$$
\mathbf a^\mathsf T\nabla^2Q\mathbf a
=
2\sum_i(a_0+a_1x_i)^2.
$$

This sum is positive for every nonzero $\mathbf a$ when the observed $x_i$
values are not all equal. Thus every movement away from the stationary point
eventually raises squared error, which establishes the unique minimum.

Before sampling, $\widehat\beta_1(\mathbf Y)$ is an estimator: a random function of the response vector. Once the observed vector $\mathbf y$ is inserted, $\widehat\beta_1(\mathbf y)$ is the numerical estimate printed below. The distinction follows the [estimator terminology](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd).

## Computing the Provo regression estimate

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-ols-by-hand
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
x <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
x_bar <- mean(x)
y_bar <- mean(y)
centered_cross_product <- sum((x - x_bar) * (y - y_bar))
centered_x_squares <- sum((x - x_bar)^2)

slope_by_hand <- centered_cross_product / centered_x_squares
intercept_by_hand <- y_bar - slope_by_hand * x_bar

provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- x
fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)

stopifnot(
  abs(slope_by_hand - coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_bits"]]) < 1e-12,
  abs(intercept_by_hand - coef(fit)[["(Intercept)"]]) < 1e-12
)

observed_ols_calculation <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "number of Provo positions",
    "mean modeled cloze surprisal",
    "mean log first fixation duration",
    "centered x-y cross-product",
    "centered x sum of squares"
  ),
  observed_value = c(
    length(x),
    x_bar,
    y_bar,
    centered_cross_product,
    centered_x_squares
  )
)
observed_ols_calculation

observed_ols_estimates <- data.frame(
  term = c("intercept", "modeled cloze surprisal"),
  estimate_by_hand = c(intercept_by_hand, slope_by_hand),
  estimate_from_lm = unname(coef(fit))
)
observed_ols_estimates
```

The contour plot evaluates the same residual sum of squares over nearby
intercept and slope candidates. Each contour joins candidate lines with the
same squared error; the fitted coefficients sit at the center of the nested
contours.

```{r}
#| label: fig-provo-ols-objective
#| fig-cap: "Residual sum of squares for nearby intercept and slope candidates in the Provo regression."
intercept_grid <- seq(
  intercept_by_hand - 0.08,
  intercept_by_hand + 0.08,
  length.out = 80L
)
slope_grid <- seq(
  slope_by_hand - 0.03,
  slope_by_hand + 0.03,
  length.out = 80L
)
ols_surface <- expand.grid(
  intercept = intercept_grid,
  slope = slope_grid
)
ols_surface$rss <- vapply(
  seq_len(nrow(ols_surface)),
  function(i) {
    sum((
      y - ols_surface$intercept[[i]] - ols_surface$slope[[i]] * x
    )^2)
  },
  numeric(1L)
)

ggplot(ols_surface, aes(slope, intercept, z = rss)) +
  geom_contour(bins = 12L, color = "#2C6E9B") +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(
      slope = slope_by_hand,
      intercept = intercept_by_hand
    ),
    aes(slope, intercept),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Candidate surprisal coefficient",
    y = "Candidate intercept"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The first table shows every observed quantity needed by the formulas. Substituting
those Provo values gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_1
&=
\frac{
`r format(centered_cross_product, digits = 7)`
}{
`r format(centered_x_squares, digits = 7)`
} \\
&=
`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`,
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\beta_0
&=
`r format(y_bar, digits = 7)`
-
\left(`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`\right)
\left(`r format(x_bar, digits = 7)`\right) \\
&=
`r format(intercept_by_hand, digits = 7)`.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the directly calculated fitted line is

$$
\widehat m(x)
=
`r format(intercept_by_hand, digits = 7)`
+
`r format(slope_by_hand, digits = 7)`x.
$$

The second table checks these direct calculations against `lm()`. The two
methods agree to numerical precision, but the formulas, rather than the software
call, define the OLS estimate.

## Deriving the estimates from a Gaussian model

The squared error calculation did not require a probability distribution. We
can arrive at the same coefficient estimates from a Gaussian model, but this
second route makes additional assumptions. Those assumptions explain why the
sum of squared errors appears in the likelihood and what the likelihood says
about the residual variance.

Condition on the observed predictor values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. Suppose that each
response has a Gaussian distribution with conditional mean
$\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$ and common conditional variance $\sigma^2$:

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).
$$

The word **common** means that the model uses the same $\sigma^2$ at every
predictor value. We also assume that the responses are conditionally
[independent](../foundations/independence.qmd). Independence allows us to
multiply the individual Gaussian densities to obtain the joint density.

Okay. So what does the likelihood look like? For candidate coefficients $b_0$
and $b_1$ and candidate variance $v>0$, the Gaussian density for response $i$
is

$$
f(y_i\mid x_i,b_0,b_1,v)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2}{2v}
\right\}.
$$

The [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the
observed $x_i$ and $y_i$ values fixed and treats $b_0$, $b_1$, and $v$ as the
values to be compared. Conditional independence gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(b_0,b_1,v;\mathbf y,\mathbf x)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
f(y_i\mid x_i,b_0,b_1,v) \\
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2}{2v}
\right\} \\
&=
(2\pi v)^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{1}{2v}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking a logarithm turns the product into a sum. Because the logarithm is
increasing, the parameter values that maximize the likelihood also maximize the
log likelihood:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell(b_0,b_1,v)
&=
\log L(b_0,b_1,v;\mathbf y,\mathbf x) \\
&=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log v
-\frac{1}{2v}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

For a fixed positive value of $v$, the first two terms do not depend on the
coefficients. The factor $-1/(2v)$ multiplying the squared error is negative.
Thus increasing the squared error lowers the log likelihood, and maximizing the
log likelihood over $b_0$ and $b_1$ gives the same coefficients as minimizing
$Q(b_0,b_1)$.

We can also see this equivalence directly from the derivatives. Differentiating
the log likelihood with respect to the two coefficients gives

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial b_0}
=
\frac{1}{v}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial b_1}
=
\frac{1}{v}
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i).
$$

Setting these derivatives to zero gives exactly the two normal equations derived
from squared error. Their solutions are therefore

$$
\widehat\beta_{1,\mathrm{ML}}
=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2}
$$

and

$$
\widehat\beta_{0,\mathrm{ML}}
=
\overline y-\widehat\beta_{1,\mathrm{ML}}\overline x.
$$

The remaining question is how to estimate the common variance. Differentiate
the log likelihood with respect to the candidate variance $v$:

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}
=
-\frac{n}{2v}
+
\frac{1}{2v^2}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

Setting this derivative to zero and multiplying both sides by $2v^2$ gives

$$
0
=
-nv
+
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

For any fixed coefficient pair, the maximizing variance is therefore the mean
squared discrepancy:

$$
\widehat v(b_0,b_1)
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

The remaining question is whether this stationary value is a maximum. The
second derivative with respect to $v$ is

$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial v^2}
=
\frac{n}{2v^2}
-
\frac{1}{v^3}
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-b_0-b_1x_i)^2.
$$

At $v=\widehat v(b_0,b_1)$, the sum of squared discrepancies equals $nv$.
Substitution gives

$$
\left.
\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial v^2}
\right|_{v=\widehat v(b_0,b_1)}
=
-\frac{n}{2v^2}<0.
$$

The log likelihood therefore curves downward in the variance direction at this
value. Substituting $\widehat v(b_0,b_1)$ into the log likelihood gives the
profile log likelihood for the coefficients:

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{profile}}(b_0,b_1)
=
-\frac n2
\left[
\log(2\pi)+1+
\log\left\{
\frac{Q(b_0,b_1)}{n}
\right\}
\right].
$$

Because the logarithm is increasing and the expression is multiplied by
$-n/2$, this profile log likelihood is largest exactly where $Q(b_0,b_1)$ is
smallest.

At the maximizing coefficients, this expression becomes

$$
\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{ML}}
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^n
(y_i-\widehat\beta_{0,\mathrm{ML}}
-\widehat\beta_{1,\mathrm{ML}}x_i)^2
=
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n}.
$$

Why does the denominator equal $n$? Maximum likelihood selects the value of
$v$ that makes the observed responses most likely after the fitted coefficients
have been inserted. Under the Gaussian model, this estimator tends to be a bit
too small on average because the same data were used to fit two coefficients.
The usual unbiased estimator corrects for those two fitted coefficients:

$$
s^2
=
\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-2}.
$$

We will derive the $n-2$ denominator from the residual degrees of freedom when
we calculate the [residual standard error](residuals.qmd#residual-standard-error).

## Computing the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimates

The coefficient estimates have already been calculated from the Provo data. We
can now insert the same observed responses into the two variance formulas.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-gaussian-mle
fitted_by_hand <- intercept_by_hand + slope_by_hand * x
ols_residuals <- y - fitted_by_hand
sse <- sum(ols_residuals^2)
n_positions <- length(y)

sigma2_mle <- sse / n_positions
sigma2_residual <- sse / (n_positions - 2L)

gaussian_log_likelihood_by_hand <-
  -n_positions / 2 * log(2 * pi) -
  n_positions / 2 * log(sigma2_mle) -
  sse / (2 * sigma2_mle)

gaussian_estimates <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "intercept MLE",
    "slope MLE",
    "error sum of squares",
    "Gaussian variance MLE: SSE / n",
    "residual variance estimate: SSE / (n - 2)",
    "Gaussian standard deviation MLE",
    "residual standard error"
  ),
  direct_calculation = c(
    intercept_by_hand,
    slope_by_hand,
    sse,
    sigma2_mle,
    sigma2_residual,
    sqrt(sigma2_mle),
    sqrt(sigma2_residual)
  )
)

stopifnot(
  abs(gaussian_log_likelihood_by_hand - as.numeric(logLik(fit))) < 1e-8,
  abs(sqrt(sigma2_residual) - summary(fit)$sigma) < 1e-12
)

gaussian_estimates
```

The table separates two quantities that answer different estimation questions.
The Gaussian maximum likelihood estimate of $\sigma^2$ uses $n$ because it
maximizes the likelihood. The residual variance estimate reported by
`summary(lm())` uses $n-2$ because it corrects the average squared residual for
the two fitted coefficients.

We can also see the coefficient maximum rather than merely reading it from the
table. For each candidate slope below, we choose its best intercept
$\overline y-b_1\overline x$ and its best variance $Q(b_0,b_1)/n$. The resulting
**profile log likelihood** is the log likelihood after those other parameters
have been maximized for that candidate slope.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-slope-profile-likelihood
#| fig-cap: "Gaussian profile log likelihood for the Provo surprisal slope. The vertical line marks the directly calculated maximum likelihood estimate."
#| fig-alt: "A concave curve of relative profile log likelihood against candidate surprisal slope, with its maximum marked by a vertical line."

profile_half_width <- max(0.01, 1.5 * abs(slope_by_hand))
slope_grid <- seq(
  slope_by_hand - profile_half_width,
  slope_by_hand + profile_half_width,
  length.out = 301L
)

profile_log_likelihood <- vapply(
  slope_grid,
  function(candidate_slope) {
    candidate_intercept <- y_bar - candidate_slope * x_bar
    candidate_sse <- sum(
      (y - candidate_intercept - candidate_slope * x)^2
    )
    candidate_variance <- candidate_sse / n_positions
    -n_positions / 2 * (
      log(2 * pi) + log(candidate_variance) + 1
    )
  },
  numeric(1L)
)

profile_data <- data.frame(
  slope = slope_grid,
  relative_log_likelihood =
    profile_log_likelihood - max(profile_log_likelihood)
)

ggplot(profile_data, aes(slope, relative_log_likelihood)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = slope_by_hand,
    color = "#8C2D2D",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Candidate surprisal slope",
    y = "Profile log likelihood relative to its maximum"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The curve reaches its maximum at the same slope obtained by minimizing squared
error. This agreement follows from the Gaussian likelihood algebra; the plot is
a check using the observed Provo responses.

## Fitting the same line with `lm()`

The call used above was

```{r}
#| label: show-provo-lm-summary
fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)
summary(fit)
```

Read the formula from left to right. `mean_log_ffd` is the response. The tilde
means “is modeled using,” and `cloze_surprisal_bits` is the predictor. The
`data` argument tells R where those two columns are stored.

The printed output contains several summaries, each of which answers a different
question:

1. `Call` repeats the model specification that R fit.
2. `Residuals` reports selected quantiles of the [residuals](residuals.qmd), the
   observed responses minus their fitted values.
3. In `Coefficients`, `Estimate` contains the same intercept and slope calculated
   above. `Std. Error` describes sampling variation in each coefficient estimate,
   while the [coefficient $t$ statistic](regression-t-statistic.qmd) divides the
   distance from a stated null value by that standard error.
4. [Residual spread](residuals.qmd#residual-standard-error) estimates the
   conditional response variation around the line. Its $n-2$ denominator gives
   the `Residual standard error`; the Gaussian variance MLE above uses $n$.
5. [$R^2$](coefficient-of-determination.qmd) compares the line's squared error
   with the squared error from predicting every response by the sample mean.
6. The [regression $F$ statistic](regression-f-statistic.qmd) compares that
   reduction in squared error with the residual spread.

The output gathers several quantities, each with its own interpretation and
sampling assumptions. At this point, we have derived only the two `Estimate`
entries. Each remaining quantity requires the additional assumptions stated in
its linked derivation.

The fitted slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_by_hand)`: one additional bit of modeled cloze surprisal corresponds to that change in the fitted word position mean of log first fixation duration. Squaring makes large vertical discrepancies count more heavily, which is one reason a few unusual responses may affect the fit.

Squared error is plausible when positive and negative deviations on the modeled scale should receive the same penalty and larger deviations should matter increasingly. This criterion comes from a working modeling decision rather than from the eye movement measurement itself. A heavy-tailed response model or absolute loss would reduce the relative influence of unusually large discrepancies.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-ols-fit
#| fig-cap: "Reader-aggregated Provo positions and the OLS conditional mean."
plot_data <- provo
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 160L)
)
grid$fitted <- intercept_by_hand +
  slope_by_hand * grid$cloze_surprisal_bits

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(plot_data, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

OLS supplies the best line under the squared error criterion. The adequacy of
that line and the dependence among passages remain open questions, which we
address through uncertainty calculations and diagnostics.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which quantity does OLS minimize?
2. Why does the slope contain cross-products of centered $x$ and $y$?
3. Which assumptions allow the Gaussian likelihood to factor into a product over observations?
4. Why do the Gaussian maximum likelihood coefficient estimates equal the OLS estimates?
5. Why does the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimate of $\sigma^2$ use $n$, while the residual variance estimate uses $n-2$?
6. What feature of squared error makes influence worth checking later?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. OLS minimizes the residual sum of squares, $\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The centered cross-products measure whether deviations in $x$ and $y$ have the same direction; dividing by centered $x$ variation converts that co-movement into change in $y$ per unit $x$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Conditional independence allows the individual Gaussian densities to be multiplied. The model also assumes a linear conditional mean and a common conditional variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. For any fixed positive variance, the Gaussian log likelihood contains the residual sum of squares multiplied by a negative constant. Maximizing the log likelihood over the coefficients therefore minimizes that sum. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. Dividing SSE by $n$ maximizes the Gaussian likelihood after the two coefficients have been fitted. Dividing by $n-2$ corrects the average squared residual for the two fitted coefficients and gives the usual unbiased residual variance estimator under the Gaussian model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
6. Squaring gives unusually large residuals disproportionate weight, so a few observations can strongly affect the fitted coefficients. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next work through the [residuals](residuals.qmd) that remain after fitting the line.
